p.t: In short
Put a **Buy now or Shop now** button right under the product, and treat every product page as a sales page.
Launch a simple page first, then improve it from customer feedback.

Check the mobile (phone) version of each page separately, and show pictures and the buy button first.
Use **Heading 6** to turn long text into boxes that open and close.

Before pasting code from a PDF, fix the broken quote marks and symbols.
Keep a product page live when stock runs out. Do not delete it.
Give each product its own page template. Otherwise, one change spreads to every product that shares it.

Test two page designs with the same ad time before you pick one.
Keep Add to Cart and Direct Buy as two separate buttons, so customers can choose.

Keep each product page **simple**: title, short benefit bullets, price, and a few proven blocks.
Check every product page on a **phone** as well as a computer before publishing.

Write your own product text, and **re-check every number** against the live price.
Test each change in the **saved preview**, then reload the live page to confirm it.

Use **Heading 6** to make a section collapsible (it opens and closes when clicked).
Most buyers see only the product page, so give it the most care.
Show reviews, FAQs and clear product facts so buyers trust the page.

Say clearly when a product needs assembly, is on back order, is pre-order, or was discontinued.
Type names exactly, because one wrong letter breaks the link.

Keep sold-out products on the site: set the stock to **zero**, and never delete them.
Give buyers **one** clear main button, and make sure it shows on mobile too.

Build **one page, then duplicate** it for each new product.
Check **every screen size** after each change.
Keep unfinished pages as **drafts** until the layout is done.
Product page structure and conversion layout

Build the product page in this order:
1. Product title and images.
2. A **Buy now or Shop now** button, placed directly under the product, with an Add to cart button above it.
3. Bundles (several items sold together as one deal), upsells (offers of a better or extra item) and urgency elements (things that push the buyer to act now, such as a countdown).

4. A short description with bullet points: **more images than text**, and simple words.
5. Customer reviews.
6. The footer (the bottom strip of the page).
Customers land on product pages, not on separate landing pages (a landing page is the first page a visitor sees after a click).
So **optimise each product page as the main landing page**, and build it to convert traffic directly (turn visitors into buyers).

Once ads are running, **send traffic to the product page, not the homepage** (traffic means visitors).
Reason: visitors can see the product and buy it immediately.

For a quick test, **a minimal viable landing page is enough** (the simplest working version of a page).
Get the page live and tested first.

Improve it from customer feedback after launch.
Do not aim for a perfect design first.
Shopify's **Dawn theme** (a free Shopify store design) includes an instant add-to-cart button for collection pages (pages that list several products).

**Enable it** in the theme settings (the controls of the store's design).
No app is needed (an app is an add-on tool).
**Place the satisfaction guarantee** (a promise to refund or replace if the buyer is not happy) high on the page, right after the key product information.

Reason: it lowers purchase risk (the chance the buyer regrets buying) early.
Visitors who are close to buying often ask: what if the product disappoints me?
Show scented or sensory products (products you smell, touch or taste) in a setting that suggests the experience, **such as on wood or among natural elements**.
Product page structure and conversion layout (continued)
**Use sharp product images** that show the product in use.
**Use tabs** (switchable sections under headings) to shrink long information, instead of forcing a long scroll (moving down the page).

Keep purchase options, reviews and key facts easy to reach from the top.
Add a **question section** below the reviews.

Keep the brand answering questions.
Reason: it shows active support and gives visitors answers without leaving the page.
Show the offer clearly:

Product price.
**Local shipping** and delivery time.
Bundle deals.

**State that stock is held in-country** (kept in the same country as the buyer).
Competitor copying (copying a rival store's page):
Copying a competitor's product page **exactly** can beat a heavily edited version in some stores.
It can bring a higher CTR (click-through rate: the share of people who click) and a lower CPM (cost per 1,000 views of an ad).

In one case, extra editing and polish **reduced sales**.
Results vary by product.
**Test each added feature separately** to see whether it increases sales.
Examples: a sticky add-to-cart bar (a bar that stays on screen while you scroll), a gift option, or colour swatches (small colour dots to pick a version).

Check these features when comparing themes.
**Include product identifiers** in a dedicated section (its own separate block).
Identifiers are codes that name the item, such as SKU (the store's own product code), UPC (Universal Product Code: the barcode number) or part number.

Reason: customers can search for the item by part number.
For fashion stores, **add a size guide**.
Size problems were a likely cause of a chargeback (the buyer asks their bank to reverse the payment) on one fashion store, even though a size guide was present.
Mobile product pages
On phones (mobile screens), **a long block of text before the product image** hurts the first impression (what a visitor thinks in the first seconds).

Lead with visuals and the buy action, not paragraphs of details.
Mobile needs an **adaptive layout** (a layout that rearranges content for each screen size).
It should not be a shrunk desktop page (the computer version, made smaller).
Keep the product name, what it does or smells like, testimonials (customer quotes) and the quantity selector (the box to pick how many) **above the fold** (the part visible before scrolling).
**Check the mobile version separately** from desktop (the computer version).
Sections, images and paragraphs may show differently or be missing on mobile.

Cross-check (compare both versions) and **add missing elements** to the mobile layout.
PageFly (a page builder app: a tool for building page layouts without code).
**Check each section on both versions** when a PageFly product page differs between desktop and mobile.
Where layouts differ, **apply the same customisation on mobile** by selecting the image and pasting the text.

Layout options in the Shopify theme editor (the tool that changes how the store looks), older, Source B 2021-22:
3 columns.
2 columns with medium image.

A further 2-column option.
The 3-column layout shows as several columns on desktop only.
**Mobile always stacks into one column** (items sit one under the other).
A two-column layout with a medium image is the traditional e-commerce layout (the usual online shop look) and **a sensible default**.
Headline, offer and trust elements
Standard Shopify product page:
The product title **stays the H1** (the page's main heading) for SEO (search engine optimisation: getting found on Google).

The product title sits at the top, with price and image.
A headline placed above the product description becomes the H2 (a second-level heading).

The H2 **must not replace the product title**.
Traditional sales page (older, Source B 2021-22: a long page that persuades step by step):

The headline is the H1 and **the first thing a visitor sees**.
The price usually comes at the **end** of the sales message on this page type.

Landing pages need **a strong offer**.
They also need several trust elements (things that build confidence) such as reviews and guarantees.

They need persuasive copywriting (words that push a reader to buy).
The source mentions five key elements but does not list them.
Free gift on a product page:
1. **Lead the product description with text about the product**, because search engines read the opening text.
2. Below the main text, embed (place inside the page) a **large image** that says the gift is free, shows the gift and states its value.
3. The image should make clear the customer receives the gift free when ordering from the store.
Product-page graphics, such as feature icons (small symbols that show key points), can be made by a designer.
They can be **hard-coded** (written directly into the site's code) instead of installing an app.
**Back up the code** (save a copy) before editing, or hire a developer on Upwork (an online freelancer marketplace) to do it.
Duplicated description text (the same text appears in the description and the specifications section):
**Contact a Shopify developer** (a programmer who works on Shopify stores).

Find developers certified by Shopify on Fiverr.com or StoreTasker.com (freelancer sites).
Check spam folders (junk mail) for replies.
Product information settings (theme editor)
Product Information block (one box of content on the page), recommended settings:

Enable sticky content on desktop: **On**.
Desktop media width: **Medium**. Media means images and video.

Constrain media to screen height: **On (Original)**. Constrain means limit the size so the pictures fit the screen.
Advanced settings are **not needed** at this stage.
Product Information subsection settings:

Variant Picker: **Pills** (buttons shaped like pills that pick a variant). A variant is a version of a product, such as a size or colour.
Quantity Selector: **Enabled**.

Sharing buttons: **Enabled**.
Description placement: **Next to Add to Cart button**.

Buy Buttons: Show dynamic checkout buttons: **On** (express buttons that let buyers pay quickly).
SKU label: **"SKU"**

**Price on product pages cannot be hidden.**
When a Compare-at price (the old, higher price) is set, it shows automatically, crossed out, to show the discount.
**The product title is pulled from the product name** and cannot be edited in the theme customizer (the store design tool).
The vendor field (the brand or supplier name) is dynamic (it updates by itself), so it updates automatically when real supplier brands are added.

For demo stores (test stores not used for real sales), **hide these Product Information subsections**:
Expiring Coupon (a discount code with a deadline).

Estimated Delivery (the expected delivery date).
Promo Image/Sale Banner (a sale picture or strip).
Inventory Status (the stock level text).

Trust Badges (small logos that build confidence).
Related Products section (the box of suggested items):
It displays "You may also like".
It lets you edit section text, layout, colours and number of products shown.

For demo stores, **hide it temporarily** with the eyedropper/hide icon (the small icon that hides an item).
Re-enable it later.
Stock levels on product pages:
1. Open Online Store (the Shopify menu for store design) > Themes > Customize.
2. Use the drop-down (a menu you open with a click) at the top (Home page) and choose Products > Default product > Product information.

3. **Click the eye icon** next to Inventory status to hide it.
4. **Do not delete the element**, so it can be restored later.
Product information settings (theme editor) (continued)
Inventory (stock count) numbers can be entered in Shopify even when they are not live (not shown to buyers).
Use **a placeholder value per product** (a fill-in number that is not the real count), for example 10 or 100.
This lets the inventory status be hidden on product pages, while the back end (the admin side buyers do not see) still tracks stock.
Shopify has no built-in field (a ready-made box) for product availability dates.
**Add the availability or backorder date as text** on the product page (a backorder is an order taken for an item that is out of stock).
Shopify free-shipping badge (a small label that says free shipping):
**Go to Online Store > Themes > Customize > Products**, select a product and look for free shipping under availability.

If it is not there, it may have been added to custom code (code written by hand) or another setting.
**Ask Shopify support.**
Product page template edits for notes:
Under the theme's product template (the layout file that shapes product pages), **add a note near the Add to cart button**.
For a back-order note, insert it in the product template near that button.

PDF manuals (2022, older; a PDF is a document file, a manual is an instruction booklet):
**Upload the file** to the Files section in Shopify.

Then add a link to it on the product page or in the description.
Product comparison table:

**Build a simple table** with attributes (features such as size or colour) in rows and products in columns.
No specialised app (a special add-on tool) is required.

Editing product templates:
In the theme editor, the product template shows as **Default product**.
In the sidebar (the side settings panel), add, remove or reorder the variant selector, quantity selector, product recommendations (suggested products)

and announcement bar (the strip at the top of the site).
**Preview before publishing** (check how it looks before it goes live).
Product information settings (theme editor) (continued)
Customising colours with custom CSS (CSS is code that sets colours and layout), for example the colour of struck-through MSRP prices (MSRP is the suggested full price, shown crossed out):

1. **Ask ChatGPT** (an AI chat tool) or another AI tool to generate CSS for the specific change.
2. Copy the generated CSS.

3. In Shopify, go to Online Store > Themes > Customize > Custom CSS.
4. Paste the CSS and **save and publish**.
Quantity selector:
If a supplier (the company that provides the items) sells in a fixed quantity (only in set amounts, such as a 6-pack), **set the default quantity selector to the most common purchase amount**.
Base the default on what top competitors show.
**The file upload option** in the theme lets customers upload files directly from the product

Example: a design or photo for a custom product (made to order for the buyer).
This avoids a separate app for collecting files.
Line item properties (extra details saved on one item in an order) store customer input, such as an engraving (words cut into the item) name, and display it on the Shopify order.
A standard supplier order usually carries only variant details.
So the property **must be mapped to the supplier's API** (the link that lets two systems exchange data) to reach them.
Line item properties can be generated **dynamically** (automatically) from Shopify metafields (extra data fields for products or customers).
The supplier's system **must recognise the parameter** (the piece of data it receives), or the data is lost.
**Developers are still needed** for complex functions (features that work like a program), such as a bundle builder (a tool where buyers build their own set).
Page builders like Replo and PageFly (drag-and-drop page tools) generally cannot produce these, as they cannot produce complex functions.
Simple landing pages and stock themes (ready-made store designs) with page builders **can be enough** for brands that do not focus on branding (building a name and look).
A simple custom engraving or name field built by a developer was roughly estimated at **about $30**.

A complicated setup or a poorly built theme can cost much more.
This figure is a rough guess, not a quote (a fixed price offer).
Descriptions and formatting
Expandable sections (boxes that open and close) in the Manhattan theme (a store design), using Heading 6 (H6, a small heading style):

1. Shopify Admin (the store's back office) > Products > select the product.
2. Highlight section headers (for example Key Features, Why You'll Love It, Specifications).

3. Change the heading format to **Heading 6** (H6).
4. Remove divider lines (lines between sections) between sections.
5. Click Save.

**Heading 6** creates expandable sections in the Manhattan theme.
This keeps long descriptions readable and organised.
Creating expandable tabs with Heading 6:
1. In the product description editor (the box where the text is written), highlight a section heading (for example Description).

2. Click the formatting dropdown (a menu for text style), currently showing Paragraph (normal text).
3. **Select Heading 6**.
4. Click Save.

5. Repeat for other sections (Key features, Specifications).
6. **Click Preview** (see the page as a buyer sees it). Sections now collapse and expand when clicked.
**Heading 6** formatting with Manhattan presents long product information cleanly, without overwhelming customers.

It improves both usability (how easy the page is to use) and page digest (how quickly a visitor can scan it).
Expanded state in Manhattan:

**The first section (the description) opens by default.**
All other sections stay collapsed (closed) and open only when clicked.

Optional Description toggle (a box that opens and closes):
**Add a new heading** labelled Description.
Set it to Heading 6.

Place it above the main product description.
Theme customisations apply to all product pages:
1. Shopify Admin > Online Store > Themes > Customize.

2. Change the page selector from Home page to Products > Default Product.
3. **Make customisations**, which then apply to all product pages.
ChatGPT-generated descriptions (text made by an AI chat tool) with bullet points often show **misaligned or badly spaced bullets** when pasted into Shopify's description editor.

Fix this:
Highlight the affected text.
Remove the bullet formatting from the editor menu.
Reapply the bullets.
Copywriting prompt (2024; a prompt is an instruction typed into an AI tool):
Descriptions and formatting (continued)
Please act as a direct response copywriter.
Write a product description for [product name] and/or [product URL] using this format: a headline; a one to three sentence description; a features and benefits section; and bullet points.
Base every feature and claim on the supplier information provided, and do not invent specifications.
Note: the prompt above is the verbatim text (word for word) of; covers the custom-made product page that uses the description.
Product description template (seasonal one-size product, 2026). **Fill every bracket** with facts about the product and your actual policies before publishing. A template is a fill-in text pattern.
One size means one size fits all.
[PRODUCT NAME] is one of the best [PRODUCT TYPE] for [SEASON]. [MATERIAL AND FEEL, e.g. soft, warm, high quality]. [SIZE STATEMENT, e.g. one size that fits most adults, stated only
if true]. [RETURN AND EXCHANGE PROMISE, only if your policy supports it]. [SHIPPING TIME, e.g. fast shipping to the USA].
Product description template (core strengths and technical details). **Replace the bracketed fields** with product facts:
The [Product Name] merges durability, practical utility, and contemporary design to address [specific need or use] with reliable performance and extended product longevity.
Core Strengths: Robust Material Composition: Fabricated from premium-grade [material] engineered for sustained use and extended lifespan.
Adaptable Use Cases: Performs effectively for [common use] while remaining suitable for [secondary uses].
Refined Aesthetic: Incorporates current design trends with a clean profile that integrates naturally across different environments.
Accessible Operation: Straightforward to use with included documentation for setup and reference.
Environmentally Responsible Manufacturing: Produced using sustainable methods designed to reduce ecological footprint.
Technical Details: Size: [Length] x [Width] x [Height] Mass: [Weight] Composition: [Material Type]
Expandable tabs, accordions and policy blocks
Accordions (boxes that open and close, like expandable sections).
Typical product page tabs: description, specifications (the list of product details), shipping info, warranty (a promise to repair or replace for a set time)

and price match guarantee (a promise to match a lower price elsewhere).
**Copy the supplier's warranty text**, but swap the contact email for your own.

Built-in tabs: the new Charlotte theme (a Shopify store design) includes product tabs.
**No tab app is needed.**

An alternative tab app (an add-on tool) costs about $5 per month.
Tabs built with the theme's own code keep the page **lighter and faster** (less data to load).

Use apps only for features too hard to code directly.
Accordion setup in Visually (an app for page design; Source E 2025-26):

**Auto-expand** the details accordion on page load (when the page first opens), only for first-time visitors.
Leave the details collapsed by default for returning customers.

Implementation (setting it up) requires **3 clicks** in Visually.
Policy blocks in the Manhattan default template (2024):
1. Shopify Admin > Online Store > Themes > Customize.

2. Change the dropdown from Homepage to Products.
3. Click into the Default Product template.

4. **Click Add Block** and select Collapsible Row (a box that opens and closes).
5. Drag it under the product description.

6. Change the title to Shipping Policy or Price Match Policy.
7. Add the content text in the editor.
8. Choose an icon (checkmark, heart, etc.).

9. **Click Save.**
10. Repeat steps 4 to 9 for additional policies. Because this is the default template, **it applies to all product pages**.
Policy information (2025):

To add policy information, go to the theme editor, click customise, select the collection or product template, and add sections using rich text (formatted text) or collapsible content (boxes that open

and close).
Include financing (pay-over-time options), customer support, return policy and price match information as expandable sections.

**Drag them below the product images** and save.
Accordions can hold an extra paragraph, such as a free shipping reminder placed below the description and dimensions.
This is a theme-level change (a change to the whole store design) and **usually needs the theme developer**.
Tabs on product pages compress (shrink) long information and keep purchase options, reviews and key facts near the top.
Duplicated descriptions in the default product layout: see under Product page structure.
Supplier-specific product page templates
Create a template per supplier (a separate page design for each supplier):

1. In the theme editor, click the Default product template.
2. Click Create template.
3. Name the template after the supplier (example: Brand B).

4. Base it on the Default product template.
5. Save the new template.
6. Expand Product information.

7. Enable and edit the Estimated delivery settings.
8. **Set a custom delivery window** for this supplier (example: 7-14 days).
9. Save changes.

Assign the template to products:
1. Go to Shopify Admin > Products.
2. Select a product from the target supplier.

3. Scroll to the Theme template field (the box that picks the layout a product uses).
4. **Select the correct template name** for that supplier (example: Brand B).
5. Save the product.
Product templates control estimated delivery dates, coupon display variations (different ways a discount code is shown) and other layout and content changes as needed.

Slower or custom-made products that cannot be returned:
Go to the theme editor.
**Duplicate the default product page template** (make a copy).

Rename the copy (for example custom made or supplier).
Change the delivery estimate and returns text there.
Then assign that template to the affected products.

Shipping or lead-time differences (lead time is the time from order to shipping; 2021, older):
1. In the theme code, duplicate the product page template.

2. Give the copy a clear name, such as product page template followed by a number.
3. Change the tabs or shipping-date information in the copy.

4. Assign the new template to the products with longer shipping times.
Note: and are identical units (copies of the same text) and are merged here.

Warranty templates (2024):
1. Go to Shopify Admin > Online Store > Themes > Customize.
2. Switch to Products.
3. Click Create Template.

4. Name the template after the supplier and warranty type (for example Supplier ABC 90-day).
5. Click Create Template.
6. Add Block > Collapsible Row.
Supplier-specific product page templates (continued)

7. Rename it to Warranty Information.
8. Add the warranty details in the content editor.
9. Save.
10. Repeat for each warranty duration (90-day, 1-year, 3-year, 5-year).
11. **Assign each product to the correct template** from the template dropdown on the product page.

12. Multiple templates allow different warranty information on different products.
Product page template without free shipping (2025):

1. In the theme customizer, open the product page template.
2. Click Default product, then Products, scroll to the bottom and click Create template.
3. Name the new template, for example no free shipping.
4. **Change every reference to free shipping** on the page (such as an offer saying free shipping) to a different offer, for example 10% off.

5. Save and check the page for any other free shipping references.
6. Assign this template to all products from the brand that cannot ship free.

The announcement bar can still say that most products ship free.
Free-gift offer placed elsewhere on the page (2025):
1. Go to Products and create a template based on the default product page, named for the offer.
2. Click Add section, choose Image with text and drag it to the desired position.

3. To add a block under the discount code, hover over the expiring coupon block, click the plus and add a block with text or Custom Liquid (a box for custom code, written in Shopify's Liquid language).
4. Save, then **assign the template** to the products that should show the offer.

Shipping selection dropdown: default to **free curbside drop-off at $0** (the item is left at the kerb, outside the door), with paid options such as in-home delivery at $100 and second-floor delivery at $300,

explained next to the dropdown.
Copy warranty text from a supplier but swap the contact email for your own.
Variant descriptions and variant selection
Decide whether variants appear **on one page or on separate product pages**.
Check the top two or three future competitors (rival stores you expect to face) in the niche (a narrow market), and copy their approach.
**Default to one page with variations** when the leaders (the strongest rival stores) use variants.
Standard and premium versions (different materials and build quality):
Look at how the top Google Shopping results (product listings on Google) display them.
Copy their structure (one page with variants or separate pages), **but write your own words**.
Bold Product Options: an app (an add-on tool) that lets customers choose custom sizes and materials on the product page.

Preset option values (choices set in advance) can update the price in real time (instantly).
Free-text entry (a box where buyers type their own answer) may not.
**Check with the app's support** before relying on it.
A single Canva image (made in Canva, a simple design tool) of colour swatches (small colour samples) does not let customers click a colour and add that variant to the cart.
**Clickable swatches** need variant options (choices built into the product), typically through an app (2025).
Set up variant-specific descriptions (a description for each version of a product) in this order:
1. Create a variant metafield (an extra data field stored for each version) named "Variant description" with type Rich text.
2. Create a snippet (a small reusable piece of code) named "variant-description" and **paste the complete corrected snippet code** into it.
3. Create a new product page template, hide the "Description" block, add a Custom Liquid block and paste {% render 'variant-description' %} into it.
4. Assign the new product page template to every product that has variants.
The variant metafield "Variant description" (type Rich text, meaning formatted text with bold, lists and links) stores formatted text separately for each variant.
The snippet reads it as custom.variant_description and outputs it with the metafield_tag filter (a Shopify code helper that formats the output).
Variant descriptions and variant selection (continued)

The snippet shows the selected variant's own description.
It **falls back to the main product description** when that variant has none.
If the resulting text is empty, the description container (the box that holds the text) is hidden entirely.
**Hide the default Description block** on the new product page template, so only the variant-description snippet displays the text.

Insert the snippet through a Custom Liquid block.
**Assign the new template only to products with variants.**
Single-variant products have no variant selector (the choice box), so the script (a small program in the page) keeps its initial render (its first display) and does not update.

**Do not use unscoped selectors** (code that finds page parts without limiting the search to this one part) for the variant ID input (the hidden box that stores the selected version's number) or the section.
Without section.id scoping (limiting code to this section by its unique ID), quick-add forms (small add-to-cart boxes) or several products on one page can receive wrong variant updates.

The script must update the description in **three cases**:
When the product form changes (the buyer's options).
When theme JavaScript (the store design's code) changes the hidden variant ID value.

Zoom suits high-resolution photos (sharp, large pictures). Low-resolution (not sharp) or AI-generated demo images look poor when zoomed. AI is software that creates pictures or text.

Choose the option that fits your image quality.
For the mobile layout, set the mobile image behaviour to **none** for AI-generated, low-resolution demo images.
Set the mobile media display to **show thumbnails**.
To adjust image zoom on product pages, go to **Shopify admin** (the back office where you manage your store) > Online Store > Themes > Customize.
Change the dropdown from Homepage to **Product page**. Then use the left navigation to set the zoom options.
Product image behaviour in the theme editor: under Online Store > Customize > Products > Default product, change the image settings (for example how media fits).

**Save**, then check the result on the store.
Images added to the product description should scale automatically for both desktop and mobile.
If they look wrong on one device, check how the image was uploaded. A correctly uploaded image **resizes itself**.
Media and images (continued)
Lazy loading (images load only when the visitor reaches them) on product variant images can stop images from loading.
If this happens, **contact the page builder support** (a page builder is a tool for designing pages; PageFly in this case).

Report that images are not loading on the page, while they work elsewhere.
**Avoid putting videos** in the product media, because they slow down page load times.
If you do use a video, the loop-after-end option (it repeats the video once it ends) restarts it automatically once it finishes.
Short animated GIFs (a GIF is a short looping animated picture) can be made by cutting a **1 to 3 second** segment from an existing video ad and exporting it as a GIF.
Keep GIFs under the size limit of **around 800 KB** (KB means kilobytes, a unit of file size). This avoids slowing the page.
Add **GIFs or short demos** to the product description so customers understand how the product works.
A visual explanation shortens the path to purchase (the steps from looking to buying).
Making a collapsible description section without code:
1. In the product editor, highlight the heading text in the description, for example Specs.
2. Open the dropdown above the description box in the rich text editor (the text box with formatting buttons). By default it shows Paragraph.
3. Select **Heading 6**, a small heading style. This turns the highlighted text into a Heading 6.
4. The heading becomes the visible top tab (a clickable title). All content below it, up to the next chosen heading, sits inside the collapsible section.

If you do not know code, use the rich text editor for headings and collapsible sections.
Do this **instead of editing the HTML** (the code behind a web page).

When a store suddenly looks broken, check first whether **recently pasted code** caused it.
Creating expandable sections:

1. Type the section title in the product description, for example Shipping, followed by its text.
2. Highlight the title text.

3. Open the format dropdown and choose **Heading 6**.
4. Make the title bold to match the other titles.
5. Click **Save and preview**. The title is now a collapsible section.
Product descriptions and collapsible tabs (continued)

Repeat for each section. The description is expanded by default.
Only text formatted as **Heading 6** becomes its own collapsible section.

Plain text stays inside the default Additional info section.
Changing an existing description section into an expandable block (Manhattan theme):
1. Open the product in the Shopify admin and go to the description editor.

2. Select the heading of the section you want to collapse, e.g. Key features, and change its format from Heading 3 to **Heading 6**.
3. Save the product.
4. Repeat step 2 for every other section heading that should collapse, e.g. Why you'll love it and Specifications.
5. Delete the horizontal divider lines (the lines between sections) that were created, then save again.
6. Open the product page preview (a view before going live) to check the result.
7. If the description intro has no heading above it, add a heading such as Description and format it as Heading 6. It then becomes the first expandable block.
In the Manhattan theme, any text set as Heading 6 becomes an expandable and collapsible block.

That block controls everything beneath it, **until the next Heading 6**.
Each block that should collapse **needs its own Heading 6**.
The first Heading 6 block on a product description is expanded by default. The visitor sees at least one section open.
Plan the first section so the most important text is **visible without a click**.
The editor view can look broken after a heading is changed to Heading 6. The product page still shows it correctly.

**Always judge the result in the saved product page preview**, not in the editor.
Leftover horizontal divider lines between description sections make the layout look messy.
**Delete them and save again** before previewing.
Build **three** collapsible tabs for the product page. They are usually labelled How it works, What's inside and Satisfaction guarantee.
Each tab should answer one buying question, such as what the buyer gets, how it is used and what protects the purchase.
Product descriptions and collapsible tabs (continued)
Place detailed product content inside collapsible drop-down menus. This includes the description, ingredients, how it is made and what is in the box.
This keeps SEO-rich text (text with search keywords, the words shoppers type into Google) on the page. It does this **without overwhelming the customer**.
Product page sections such as measurements, shipping, returns and price match (a promise to match a lower competitor price) are fine in moderation.

**Four to five** dropdowns or headers is not too many.
Product description order: set up the product description first, then the features.
The description goes first because Google Merchant Center (Google's product list tool, called Merchant Center here) reads it first.

The features follow for extra keywords.
Use the supplier's product description as a starting point.
**Check that it is complete and accurate** before publishing the product page.
Write **unique product sales copy** for each product, rather than using supplier copy (the text the supplier provides).
Add size, colour and variant charts. Offer downloadable PDF files (documents you can save and print), such as warranty terms and installation instructions.
Shopify's built-in AI suggestions for product descriptions should **not be accepted blindly** (accepted without checking).
They do not follow a product page SEO approach. Use them only as a starting point and optimise the result yourself.
Write the **product map** first. Then fill the product description field in the Shopify product editor from it.
A blank description box with no guide causes writer's block (being stuck with no words). The map gives you the material to fill that field.

Starting a product description for a test store (procedure):
1. Open the description of a proven competitor product (a rival store selling the same thing).

2. Copy its structure, such as the sections and their order.
3. Rewrite the wording and improve it for your own store, keeping the structure that the competitor uses.
Build specification tables (tables of product details, such as size and weight) with Shopify's **native editor** first. Native means built-in, coming with Shopify.
Product descriptions and collapsible tabs (continued)

Third-party apps (add-on tools made by other companies) can slow the site.
Use custom HTML (your own code) **only if** the native editor cannot produce the table.
Embed a supplier video in a product description. An embed code is a short code that shows a video from another site.

Copy the embed code, typically from YouTube, and paste it into the description.
**No developer** (a person who writes code) is needed for this step.
Bullet points in the product description that wrap onto a second line can break their indentation in Shopify.

A line of CSS (styling code) from the Shopify forum (an online help board) can fix the layout.
Standard Shopify variants share **one product description**.
A description that differs by colour will **not change** when the customer selects another variant.

Solving this needs an app or custom code. So **test each variant in the preview** before launch.
Older tab setup with the Easy Tabs app:

1. Open the Easy Tabs app and start the free trial if prompted.
2. Under Standard tabs, click Configure default tab. This builds standard tabs from the product description.
3. Choose the tab title for the default tab (for example Description). Or keep the text before the first heading as separate text above the tabs.

4. Click Next. Then choose the text below the tabs, or select Don't need text below the tabs.
5. Click Next and check the live preview.

6. Under Static Tabs (tabs with fixed content you write yourself), click Add Static Tab. Enter the title and content for each tab. At minimum, include shipping and why buy from us. Click Save static tab.

7. Open Settings and adjust Layout. This covers padding (the empty space inside a box) and colours. Then click Save.
Standard tabs are built from the product description.
Each heading tagged as H5 (a heading level 5) becomes a tab title.
The content after that heading becomes the tab content. The app splits the product description into separate tabs this way.
Text placed before the first heading can become a default tab with its own title, such as Description.

Or it can stay as separate text above the tabs widget (the tab box).
**Choose one option on purpose**, so the first thing a shopper reads is clear.
Variants, buttons and add-to-cart
Use Shopify's **default variant buttons** for colour options.

They show the colour name and change the product image on click.
True colour swatches (small colour squares) require custom code or a swatch app.

Native Shopify **does not change** the add-to-cart button colour based on the selected variant.
This needs a third-party app and is not a standard feature.
Variants shown in the video must be set up as **real product variants** in Shopify.
The shopper selects a variant in the video and checks out through the store's native checkout (Shopify's built-in payment page).
A variant that is not configured in the store **cannot be sold** through the video.
The add to cart button text changes to **"view cart"** after the button is clicked. Keep that setting on.
Avoid heavy customisation of the buttons before supplier approval. Little is needed at that stage.

Buy buttons settings: turn on **"Show dynamic checkout buttons"**.
Keep the two options below it **off**.
"Customise add to cart" and "Enable add to cart icon" are optional. If turned on, the button colours can be changed under the buy buttons settings.
The Buy with Shop Pay button (Shop Pay, Shopify's fast checkout) only appears when Shopify Payments (Shopify's own payment service) is enabled for that store.
Demo or test stores without Shopify Payments **will not show it**.
Model the product page structure on the **top two or three competitors** selling the same product.
If they use one page with variants, use one page with variant options. If they use separate pages per size, do the same.
Google Merchant Center can still submit each variant as its own product.
Cart behaviour
The cart type options are: dropdown confirmation, slide-out cart, pop-up modal (a box that appears on top of the page),

redirect to the cart page (send the visitor straight to it), and skip cart and go directly to checkout.
The checkout is the payment step.

**Dropdown confirmation** is a suitable default when starting out.
The other options can be tested later.

After add-to-cart, most stores send shoppers **straight to checkout**.
Keep them on the product page **only when customers are likely to add several items**.

Sticky add-to-cart bar, Manhattan theme: go to Online Store > Themes.
Click **Customise** next to Manhattan. Open Product and the default product page.
Click the Buy buttons block, **switch off "Sticky add to cart"**, and click Save.
About **90-95%** of store traffic (visitors) lands on the product page.

Only about 5-10% goes to the homepage or collection pages.
The product page is therefore the most important page to optimise.
For a niche store (a store for one small market) with many similar products, a single-product landing page usually converts better than a collection page.

Conversion means a visitor buying. A landing page is a page built to get one sale.
A single-product landing page removes choice friction (too many choices slow buying).
It also continues the emotional journey from the ad. Variants can cover near-identical products.

**Pre-fill the selector with the most popular choices, so about 80%** is already chosen.
The customer keeps about 20% agency (the feeling of choosing for themselves).
This reduces the feeling of filling out a form from scratch.
For a variant selector with many options and product cards (small boxes showing each product), start with a **drop-down** rather than a pop-up.

A pop-up is harder to use for a complex choice.
It can hide the options a shopper needs to compare.
Product page order:

1. Show the product title.
2. Show a short two to three line description that explains the product.
3. Show reviews.
Product page layout and conversion (continued)
4. Show the variant or option selector in a compact form, on one line where possible.
5. Place the add-to-cart button above the fold (the part of the page visible without scrolling), with the price visible near it.

Below the product box, add landing-page style sections that tell the brand or product story.
Examples are multi-column, image and text, rich text or video sections.
These can be built with Shopify section tools.
Map a product page to the proven layout, in this order: a hero (the big top section) with title bar, brand name, rating line, product name, price with savings label, three checkmark benefit bullets,
and Add to Cart with payment icons.
Then add a See it in action area with **3 to 6** product videos, 3 customer testimonials (customer reviews quoted as praise), feature blocks, a 6-question FAQ, and 3 collapsible tabs.
Keep the product page simple: product title, short benefit bullets, price and a few proven blocks.

Switching on every section the theme offers **adds mobile load** (more to load on phones).
It also adds more copy to maintain for each product.

Before publishing, check the product page on **mobile as well as desktop**.
Confirm the price, Add to Cart button, carousel, collapsible tabs and FAQ all display.

Also check that font sizes (text sizes) and spacing are readable.
Template for mapping a product page (paste the data and attached screenshots below it):
I am giving you the product page template I want (hero with title bar, brand name, rating line, product name, price with savings, three checkmark bullets, Add to Cart with payment icons,
See it in action section with three image placeholders, What our customers say with three testimonial cards, two feature blocks with headline and body, a Shop Now button, six FAQ questions,
three collapsible tabs titled How It Works, What's Inside and Satisfaction Guarantee, a floating review bubble above the collapsibles, and a newsletter section).
Using the product data and images I provide, fill every element of this template exactly, keeping the same order and the same number of blocks.
Product page layout and conversion (continued)
Do not invent statistics, review counts, sales figures, testimonials, guarantees or claims that are not in the data I provide; if a field has no data, write [MISSING: field name] instead.
Mark any figure you took from the data with its source. Testimonials must be rewritten from real customer reviews I provide and must not be fabricated.
Write the output as clean copy with headings per section, ready to paste into the theme editor. Product name: [PRODUCT NAME]. Price: [PRICE]. Compare-at price: [COMPARE-AT PRICE].
Product images and screenshots: [ATTACHED]. Product data and reviews: [PASTE DATA].
Procedure for building the page from a marketplace listing (a product page on a shared sales site):

1. Open the product page on the marketplace listing and select all text with Ctrl+A (the keyboard shortcut for select all).
2. Copy the selection with Ctrl+C (copy).
3. Open a new Claude chat (a chat with the AI assistant Claude), paste the copied listing data, and attach the reference screenshots.
4. Paste the page template prompt below the data and send it.
5. Check every price, review count and sold count in the output against the live listing and the current price.

6. Copy each output section into its matching block in the theme editor and save.
AI-generated product page copy often carries **stale numbers** (old numbers).
These are copied from an earlier product snapshot (a saved copy from one point in time), such as old review counts, old sold counts or old prices.
Before publishing, **re-check every number** against the current product data and the live price.
Video Carousel block: there are separate switches for "Enable autoplay" and "Show navigation dots".
Autoplay means the slides move on their own. Navigation dots (pagination dots) are small dots showing which slide is shown. They can be placed below the carousel.
Autoplay can distract from the buying decision. **Test it on mobile** before keeping it on.
Reviews, trust and FAQ blocks
The **customer review block** has these settings: Avatar image (the small profile photo), Review content, Reviewer name, Rating, Star colour and size,
Background, Text colour, and Drop shadow (a soft shadow behind the box).

Carousel settings (a slider you swipe through): "Enable carousel mode", "Show multiple reviews in a swipeable carousel", and Navigation dots placement (the small dots that show which review you are on).
Set each **reviewer's name and avatar** to match the reviewer's gender, so the review looks real.
Trustpilot (a public review website) rating block: set the **Rating Text** (for example Excellent), the rating value, and the Trustpilot Star colour.
Use Trustpilot's official green when you show its badge, because it is their brand colour.
The **"Use product description for question"** toggle fills answers from the product description instead of manual answers.
FAQ Appearance covers padding (space inside the box), margins (space outside the box), border radius (how round the corners are), border colour and border style.
You can store the FAQ in the footer (the bottom strip of every page).
Sections can use Background Image Mode (how a background picture fits) and Desktop Layout Options, such as centring the FAQ when there is no image.
Keep the **review stars or review block** in a visible place.
Older method (2019): move review stars or a review block under the product title in a Shopify theme (the design files that control how your store looks).
1. **Check the review app's settings first.** Many apps can show ratings under the price or title without code changes.
2. If the app has no such option, **open the theme's code editor** and open the product.liquid file (the main code file for product pages).
3. Select all of the file's code, paste it into a document, and **save it as a backup** (a safety copy).

4. Find the block that shows the reviews. The code differs for each review app.
5. **Cut** that block and paste it directly below the title markup (the code for the title).
6. **Save** and check the product page. If it breaks, paste the backup back and save.
Reviews, trust and FAQ blocks (continued)
Each brand's **warranty** (a promise to fix or replace a faulty product) should appear on every product page for that brand.
Describe its scope (what it covers) clearly, such as parts only, so buyers know what they get.
Warranty and product claims: **show the real product condition**, so buyers do not expect a finished item.
The Image with text block in a product template (a layout file that sets which sections a page shows) can hold an image, a brand name, a short brand description and a button.
Keep the button and link it to a collection (a group of products shown on one page) that holds that brand's products. Or **delete the button** and keep only the text blocks.
The Source A Shopify theme includes an ETA feature (estimated time of arrival) that shows the estimated delivery date on the product page.
The ETA can update in real time (instantly, as information changes).
For products that need assembly, **state clearly** on the product page that assembly is required.

Give an estimated assembly time, such as four hours.
Show the real product condition, so buyers do not expect a finished item.
Products that need professional installation must say so on the product page: **they must be installed by a professional.**
Customers usually hire a local installer. Offering installation yourself means finding nationwide installation companies and pricing them, which is more manual work.
For a custom feature, such as an extra multi-line text field (a box for several lines of text) under the product title, you usually need a little extra code (computer instructions).

**Hire a Shopify developer** on StoreTasker (a site for hiring experts) to build it.
Product Options is a Shopify app (an add-on tool for the store).
It adds customisable option fields, such as size, colour or personalisation inputs (boxes where the buyer types their own text), to product pages.
Product pages use separate tabs (clickable sections) named Description, Shipping and Price match.
For products from non-MAP suppliers (suppliers without a Minimum Advertised Price rule, which sets the lowest price you may show), **hide the Price match tab** on the product page.
List the excluded brands at the top of the general price match policy page (the rules for matching a lower price elsewhere).
Video on product pages
**Path to add a video** to a product description: go to Products, open the product, and use the Description editor's code view (the </> button,
which shows the raw code) to paste the script (a short piece of code).

Add a short paragraph, such as an explanation of the shoppable video (a video people can click to buy from).
Then click **Save**.
If you do not want the snippet in the description, use a Custom HTML snippet block (a block that holds your own web code) instead.
LyveCom (a video widget service) embed options: the Widget tab offers the embed code in two steps.
**Step 1: Copy the code.** Step 2: Paste the code on any page of the website.
The Embed option (direct embed) is the alternative to the floating widget (a small box that stays on screen).

Place it where the video should appear, such as a product description.
The widget snippet copied from the LyveCom dashboard (the control panel) has this structure.
The key name for the language setting was hard to read in the screenshot, so **verify it** against the copy from the dashboard before publishing.
<script src='https://dashboard.lyvecom.com/widget/widget.js'></script> <script> LyveComWidget.mount({ account: 'YOUR_ACCOUNT_ID', stories:
true, lang: 'en', position: 'left' }); </script>
The snippet can go in a product description, the Shopify page builder, a Shogun builder (a page-building app), or any block that accepts an HTML snippet (a block that takes web code;

HTML is the basic web code language).
The floating widget suits homepage greetings and new collection launches.

The product-page embed suits engagement on a single product.
Show a **See it in action** section with 3 to 6 short videos that show the product in use.

Include them in the product page carousel (a slider) with navigation dots.
Upload the video files directly in the theme block, rather than linking to outside pages.
Where videos go: the main media gallery (the row of main product photos) should avoid video, because it slows page load (how fast the page opens).

The See it in action section is the place for 3 to 6 product videos.
Use the gallery for images. Use the video section for demonstrations.
Bundles and upsells
An upsell is an extra offer that raises the order value (the total a buyer spends).
Give each product its own unique add-on option (an extra item or option added to the main product).
Where possible, take add-ons from the **same supplier**, to simplify shipping.
Google Shopping (Google's product listing service) submits the bundle price (the price of a set of products sold together) as the product price.
So use **add-on options** on the product page instead of default bundles.
The listed price stays lower, while average order value (the average amount each buyer spends) still rises.
Shrine theme supports bundles where a customer chooses different variants (versions of the same product, such as size or colour) in the bundle.
It does not upsell a different product. So a hoodie bundle can offer another colour or size, but **not a t-shirt**.

PageFly (a page builder: a tool to design pages without code) is recommended for stores with one product plus an upsell.
That product gets the most focus.
PageFly is **not recommended** for stores with many products.
PageFly is a page builder used to build advertorials (sales articles that look like news or blog posts).
It offers templates for blog-style layouts. You can customise them to look like a native editorial article (an article that fits the site's own style).

PageFly is used as the page builder for the store pages (homepage, product page, About us, Contact us).
Ryviu (a review app) is used to add product reviews.
Whether to build a PageFly landing page (a single page built to get one sale) depends on the store.
A general store selling multiple items with offers like buy two, get the third free may not need one.
Page builders (PageFly) (continued)

Testing one product at a time in a general store **does** benefit from a PageFly landing page.
Advertorial page structure:

1. **Start with the problem** the ad showed, for example a pet losing energy.
2. Educate with facts about the problem and why it happens.

3. Suggest general solutions the reader could try on their own.
4. **Introduce your product at the end** as the shortcut.
5. Add a clear call-to-action button (the button that asks for the sale), such as "Choose your package", that links to the offer page.
Back-order delivery note, Source A. A back order means the store has sold the item but has not received it yet.
This product is currently on back order until [date]. You can place your order now and pay a deposit of [amount], and we will ship it to you as soon as it arrives.

Showing a different delivery note on one product (for example a back order with a long ETA):
1. Go to **Online store > Themes > Customize**.
2. Open the product page dropdown and choose **Products**.
3. **Click Create template** and name it, for example "ETA example two months". (A template is a saved page layout you assign to chosen products.)

4. In that template, **hide the estimated delivery section** and add a Text block under the Buy it now button.
5. **Save.**

6. On the product itself, scroll to Theme template, **select the new template**, then preview it.
Back-order text (template):
Please note, this product is back ordered with an estimated arrival of [date]. You can still place your order, and we will confirm the shipping date by email after purchase.
Place a back-order ETA note **directly beside the add-to-cart button** (the button that puts the item in the basket).
Do not put it lower on the page. Shoppers must see the delay before they buy.
Out-of-stock and discontinued products
Do not delete a product page when the product is discontinued (no longer made or sold) or unavailable.
Set the inventory (the stock count) to **zero**, so no one can add it to the cart.
Add a section under the add-to-cart button that says the product is currently unavailable.
In that section, link to similar in-stock products in the same price range that ship fast.
If the supplier replaces the product with a new model, add a prominent (easy to spot) note on the old page.

The note names the new model, links to it, and states that it is in stock and ships fast.
Discontinued product with a replacement:
1. Keep the old product page live, with inventory set to **zero**.
2. **Create a new product page** for the replacement version. Submit it to shopping campaigns (paid product ads) and free listings (product results shown without paying).
3. Add a section below the cart button on the old page. It says the product was discontinued and links to the in-stock replacement, so existing SEO traffic is not lost.

(SEO is how search engines such as Google find and rank your pages. SEO traffic is visitors who arrive from search.)
Replacement note (template):

This product has been discontinued. Our updated version, [Replacement product name], is in stock and ready to ship: [link]. You may also like these in-stock options: [Product 1], [Product 2], [Product 3].

Discontinued product with no replacement:
1. **Set its inventory to zero** on the store.
2. Exclude it from shopping campaigns and organic listings (free results in search).
3. **Keep the page.** Add a section saying it has been discontinued, with two or three similar in-stock products customers might consider.
4. This keeps the SEO traffic and gives visitors somewhere to buy.
Pre-orders
Pre-order model when stock is unavailable, for example before Chinese New Year:
1. **Change the Add to cart button** on the product page so it reads "Pre-order".
2. Add a description explaining that the product sold out due to demand and when shipments restart, for example in two to three weeks.
3. **Take payment now** and ship when stock arrives.
To change the button label to Pre-order, **edit the button text** in the page builder or theme editor, if you use a page builder or a current theme.
On an old legacy theme (an older theme version), the label has to be changed manually in the Shopify theme settings.
Changing the pre-order button text on the Shopify theme (older theme method, admin path as given in the source):
1. In the Shopify admin (the store's control panel), open **Online Store**, then the theme you use. Check the exact label in your theme editor.
2. Open the theme settings and the language editing area (where the store's wording is edited). Find the button text for buy now.

3. **Change the button text** from "buy now" to "pre-order now".
4. Note that this changes the button for the **whole store**, not just one product. Check every product page afterward.
For a pre-order product, make the status clear: start the product description with a **large red line** such as "pre-order now".
Keep the setup manual. Avoid installing extra apps, because each app can slow the store down.
Pre-orders can sell well, especially in fashion (clothing), where many products are bought before stock arrives.
**Do not drop the model** based on claims that pre-orders do not work.
Product page as the main conversion page
A conversion is a visitor who buys.
About **95%** of paid-ad visitors (people who click your ads) see only the product page.
Only 3 to 5% visit the home page or collection page. So most design and offer effort belongs on the product page.
The product page shows most product details. It can be customised heavily through the theme.
A collection page displays every product assigned to that collection.
Before traffic is sent to a product page, it should include product images or videos, customer reviews and an FAQ section.
**Prioritise the landing page** (the first page a visitor lands on) over checkout tweaks. Checkout is the final payment step.
A strong landing page builds the trust that brings buyers to checkout.
Shipping information and similar details are common checkout blockers (things that stop people buying). Address them after the page works.
Every extra page or click between the landing page and checkout lowers conversion. It increases frustration and abandonment (leaving without buying).
**Shorten the path to purchase** wherever possible. Making shoppers browse longer does not help when attention spans are short.
Copy belongs on product pages, longer sales pages built with funnel tools such as ClickFunnels or Leadpages (tools for building sales pages), collection and category pages,

and marketplace listings on Amazon or eBay.
Shopify is named as the standard example of a product-page setup.
When traffic comes from TikTok, **build the store mobile first** (for phones before computers).
One estimate says nearly all TikTok buyers shop on a phone. So the desktop (computer) layout can get less attention.
Page structure and conversion elements
Top of the product page, in this order: product image, product name, USP (unique selling point, the main reason to buy),
star reviews, then four or five benefit-driven bullet lines (lines that say what the buyer gains).
Lower sections repeat the pattern: a main benefit headline, up to two lines of text, then an image or GIF (a short looping animation).
Add a **FAQ section** for problem-solving products, since almost every buyer has questions.
Add a **risk-free or 30-day money-back guarantee** section. It works well for conversion.
Remove every element unrelated to the main product, such as a "frequently bought together" block (a box suggesting other items).

Unrelated suggestions act as friction and lead visitors away.
Show a **clear size guide** on every product page.
Show the shape and fit of each item through mock-ups (drawn or staged pictures) or model images.
For oversized or drop-shoulder cuts (a shoulder seam that sits lower than usual), make the fit visible, so buyers know what will arrive.
Provide **accurate measurements** for every product category. For tops, that means chest width (across the chest), arm length and shoulder drop (how far the shoulder seam sits down).

Give the equivalent measures for trousers and jackets.

**Static tabs** are created once in the app settings. Then they are added to all products or to selected collections.

A variant is one version of a product, such as a specific size or colour.
p.h: Variant descriptions: When to use them

p.t: Variant-specific descriptions are only worth setting up when the variants differ enough that one shared description does not fit them.
If the variants share the same details, a **single default description** covering all variants works without extra setup.
Create the variant metafield definition. A metafield is an extra data field you add to Shopify.
Setting: **Settings > Metafields and metaobjects > Variants (under Metafield definitions) > Add definition**.
Name the definition **'variant description' and set Select type to Rich text (text with formatting, such as bold). Then click Save**.
Shopify creates the key custom.variant_underscore_description (the internal name Shopify gives the field). The name must match exactly, including spelling, lowercase and underscores.
Setup procedure (continued)

1. **Log into the Shopify admin.**
2. Click **Settings**.
3. Click **Metafields and metaobjects**.

4. Scroll to the bottom of the list and click **Variants** under Metafield definitions.
5. Click **Add definition**.
6. Enter the name **'variant description'**.

7. Click **Select type and choose Rich text** (search for it if it is not visible).
8. Click **Save**.

9. Check that the Metafields and metaobjects overview now shows one definition for variants instead of zero.
Enter a description for each variant:

1. Go to Products and open a product that has variants.
2. Leave the product page and open it again, so the variant fields refresh.

3. Scroll down to the Variants section and expand the list.
4. Click one variant, for example 'seven foot blue'.

5. Scroll to the field named variant description and click it to open the text box.
6. Enter the description for that variant and click **Save**.

7. Repeat for every other variant.
To edit later, follow the same path and change the text.

Create the snippet that reads the variant description. A snippet is a small reusable piece of code.
1. Go to **Online Store > Themes**.

2. Click the three-dot button next to the theme you use and choose **Edit code**.
3. Expand the Snippets folder to see the existing snippets.

4. Click the first icon in the toolbar, **New file**.
5. **Name the file variant_description.liquid.**
6. Open the new file, paste the snippet code, and click **Save**.

The file name has to match the name used in the Custom Liquid block later.
Create the custom product page template:

1. Go to **Online Store > Themes and click Customize** (not Edit code).
2. In the top dropdown, choose **Home page**, then select **Products**.
3. Open the template dropdown at the top. Most stores only show the template named default product.

4. **Create a new template**, name it **'variants with unique descriptions'**, and base it on the default product template.
5. Click **Create template**.

A newly created product template is assigned to zero products. Creating it does not change any live product page.
It only takes effect on products you assign to it manually.
Setup procedure (continued)

Prepare the template layout:
1. In the left panel of the new template, **hide the Description section** so the default description no longer shows.

2. Hover just below the Description area until a blue line with a plus sign appears.
3. Click **Add block and choose Custom liquid** (a block that runs code you type).
4. In the code box that opens on the right, enter: render variant description
5. Scroll down in the preview to check that the first variant's description appears, then click **Save**.
The Custom Liquid block displays the code you type into it.
The entry 'render variant description' tells it to load the snippet variant_description.liquid.

So the block name in the code must match the snippet file name without the.liquid extension.
Assign the template to the product:
1. Go to Products and open the product that has the unique variant descriptions.
2. Scroll down on the right side to the **theme template** setting, which shows the template the product currently uses.

3. Click the current template and select **'variants with unique descriptions'**.
4. Click **Save**.

Only the products you assign change. Every other product page keeps its previous template.
Test the variant descriptions:

1. Open the product and click **Preview**.
2. Scroll to the product details and click each variant option, for example seven foot blue.

3. Check that the description and the image change to match the selected variant.
4. Click the other variant options, such as eight foot green, and check each one.
Field names, the definition name and the snippet file name **must be typed exactly**.
Differences in spelling or capital letters break the connection between the metafield, the snippet and the template.
Copy the names from this handbook rather than typing them from memory.
Product information settings
In Shopify (the software that runs your online shop), open the theme editor (the tool that controls how the shop looks) and the product settings. Set:

Sale badge style to **Save $10** (the small label that shows the saving).
Option style to Selectable boxes (clickable boxes for choosing, such as a size).

Display stock levels to **Hidden**.
Quick shop button to **Disabled**.
In the Shopify theme product settings, **enable color swatches** (small color dots a buyer clicks to pick a color).
Leave the other product settings at their **defaults** (the standard settings the software starts with) while the storefront (the part of the shop visitors see) is in its early stage.

In the **Shrine theme's product information settings (a theme is a shop design template), the Active variant images** filter controls which variant images appear. A variant is one version of a product, such as one color.
The **Hide other variants' media switch only works when each variant has one** media item (one picture or video) assigned in Shopify admin (the back-office area) under Products.
If you need to hide **several** media items per variant, use the filtering setting instead.

For a simple store with **one** product:
The main button can say **"Add to bag"** or "I want it now".

It sends the visitor straight to checkout (the payment step).
This skips the cart page (the page that holds chosen items before payment), which can be a point where visitors leave.
A **sticky button** (a button that stays on screen while the visitor scrolls) lets a visitor who is already convinced act right away.
It works instead of scrolling back or leaving.
Without a visible **call to action** (a clear prompt to act, such as a buy button), visitors who are almost ready can leave before they buy.

**Case:** A store's add-to-cart rate (the share of visitors who click add to cart) was lower than expected. Visitors who read the product but did not see a button on mobile (a phone screen) were leaving.

**Action:** A sticky add-to-cart button was added to the mobile product page.
**Result: The add-to-cart rate rose by about 25%**.
In the Shopify theme product settings, **disable** the Quick shop button (a button that opens a popup with product details).
Quick shop adds JavaScript (a small program that runs in the visitor's browser) that slows the site, even when customers do not click it.
So customers should go to the full product page instead.
In the Shopify theme product settings, **show** the dynamic checkout button (a fast payment button) so each customer sees their preferred payment method, such as PayPal

or Apple Pay (online payment methods), from those available on the store.
Set the Add to cart button to **Enable on desktop only**.

**package) that needs code must be placed in the product page**

**template** (the design file for product pages).
**Bundle Bear** requires this step.

The first is about unrelated suggestions that create friction (things that slow a buyer down).
The second is about a bundle offer that the product page must present.

p.t:
and **turn on inventory tracking** (the shop counts how many items it has).
Set the stock to **zero** (out of stock) instead of deleting the product.

This stops customers from buying it.
Set a product to **zero stock** instead of hiding it.
The product stays visible on the front end (the part of the shop visitors see) but cannot be bought.

It avoids **indexing problems** (trouble with search engines, such as Google, listing the page).
It goes live again when stock is added.
Keeping out-of-stock product pages live keeps them **indexed (listed by search engines) and receiving free organic traffic** (visitors who arrive from search results, not paid ads).
The links on them can **redirect** visitors (send them automatically to another page) to in-stock products that still sell.

**Inventory tracking on, stock set to zero**
Result: Product stays live, cannot be bought, goes live again when stock is added
**Hide the product**

Result: Compared with zero stock, hiding is the option that causes indexing problems
**Delete the product**
Result: Not recommended; set zero stock instead of deleting
